inserts.title: From the Archives, Why These Levers Work
inserts.html: Psychologist Daniel Kahneman describes two modes of thought: a fast, automatic System 1 that runs on heuristics and gut feeling, and a slower, effortful System 2 that checks details and reasons things through (Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011; building on Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Every lever above is a way of keeping a target in System 1, reacting on instinct, long enough to act before System 2 has a chance to ask an inconvenient question.

inserts.title: Beyond Detection: Slowing Down the Guess Itself
inserts.html: Correlating login events after the fact, as in the function above, is one layer of defense. A second, independent layer works before any attack even starts: how the password is stored. NIST SP 800-63B (Digital Identity Guidelines), Section 5.1.1.2 “Memorized Secret Verifiers,” requires that verifiers store memorized secrets salted and hashed with a suitable one-way key derivation function, and recommends a memory-hard function specifically because it raises the cost of an offline attack. Algorithms built for this job – bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2 – include a tunable “cost” or “work” parameter that an administrator can dial up over time: each increment roughly doubles the computation required for every single guess, for both the legitimate server checking one login and an attacker checking millions offline. That per-guess cost, multiplied across a huge guess list, is what turns an offline dictionary attack from a fast batch job into an impractical one – without changing how long a real user waits to log in.

An evil twin broadcasts the same SSID as the legitimate access point, typically at higher
signal strength, so the victim's traffic routes through attacker-controlled hardware – a full
man-in-the-middle position – while the real access point never sees the connection at all.
